items.title: Rewriting a real draft letter to the public (Level 5)
items.source: GOV.UK Style Guide; GOV.UK content design guidance
items.body: In the job you will often be handed a draft written by someone else, or a standard letter that has grown over the years, and asked to improve it. A reliable method is to read the draft as the customer would. First, find the main point and ask whether it is in the first paragraph. Next, list every action the customer must take and check that each one has a deadline and a way to do it. Then look for the problems covered in plain English guidance: long sentences, the passive voice, jargon, vague words such as 'promptly' or 'in due course', and phrases that blame or confuse. Check that the letter explains why a decision was made and how to challenge it, if it is a decision letter. Check that the tone is courteous. Keep every fact that matters. Do not drop a date, a reference number, an amount or a condition when you shorten text. Do not add promises that the department has not agreed to. Keep the same terms throughout. A good rewrite normally has a short heading, an opening that states the point, short paragraphs, a bulleted list for several documents, and a closing that gives contact details and hours. Before you finish, read it aloud and compare it against the original to make sure that nothing important has changed. If you are not sure that a fact is right, ask the owner of the process rather than guessing.

questions.prompt: A draft letter begins: 'I am writing with reference to your recent correspondence, which has been given careful consideration, and to inform you that, following a review, your claim has been successful.' Which rewrite of the opening is best?

options.text: Your claim has been successful. We have reviewed your letter and will pay you £120 on 4 July.
I am writing about your recent letter. After a careful review, we have decided that your claim is successful.
Thank you for your recent correspondence, which has been carefully considered. Your claim has been successful.
Following our review of your letter, I am pleased to inform you that your claim has now been successful.

questions.hint: The best opening leads with the outcome and the next step.

questions.prompt: A draft says: 'Documents should be submitted promptly.' What is the main weakness?

options.text: The sentence should be longer, so that it sounds more official
'Documents' should always be written as 'document' here
'Submitted' is the wrong spelling for a government letter
'Promptly' is vague and gives no date for sending

questions.hint: Vague time words should be replaced by a date.

questions.prompt: A decision letter refuses a claim and says only 'Your circumstances do not meet the criteria.' Which addition would improve it most?

options.text: A sentence thanking the person for their patience again
A longer list of the rules, with their legal references
A sentence saying the decision is final and cannot be queried
The reason in plain words and how to ask for a review

questions.hint: A refusal needs a reason and a route to challenge it.

questions.prompt: While shortening a letter you notice you have dropped the sentence giving the deadline. What should you do?

options.text: Move it to a separate leaflet that is posted later on
Replace it with 'as soon as possible' to save a few words
Put the deadline back, because the reader needs that fact
Leave it out, since the letter is now shorter and clearer

questions.hint: Never remove facts that affect what the reader must do.

questions.prompt: The original letter uses 'claim' in its heading, 'application' in paragraph two and 'request' in paragraph three. What is the best fix?

options.text: Choose one term, probably 'claim', and use it throughout
Replace all of them with 'it'
Keep all three, as variety makes the letter easier to read
Use the longest term, as it is the most precise

questions.hint: Consistent terms stop readers thinking there are separate things.

questions.prompt: A draft promises 'We will always reply within five working days', but the team's real target is ten. What should you do?

options.text: Keep the promise, because it sounds helpful to customers
Check the target with the process owner and promise only that
Remove the sentence without telling the process owner
Change it to 'within a reasonable time' to avoid commitment

questions.hint: Do not promise more than the department has agreed.

questions.prompt: After rewriting a draft you read it aloud and stumble twice. What does this suggest?

options.text: The letter needs a heading in capitals to help the reader
Those sentences are probably too long or awkward
The letter should be sent without any further changes to it
The letter is perfect as it stands and can be sent now

questions.hint: Reading aloud shows where readers will struggle.

questions.prompt: You are not sure whether a figure in the original draft is correct. What is the best step?

options.text: Delete the figure from the rewrite altogether
Round the figure to the nearest ten or hundred
Ask the owner of the process to confirm it
Guess based on a similar letter you wrote

questions.hint: Facts should be checked, not guessed.

items.title: Email scenarios: subject lines, openings and closings (Level 5)
items.source: GOV.UK content design guidance; ICO guidance on personal data
items.body: Practical email skills come down to choosing the right subject line, opening and closing for the situation. Think about who the reader is, what they must do, and what could go wrong. For a request to a customer, put the action and date in the subject line: 'Send your bank statement by 6 June'. For a reply to a query, repeat the topic so the thread is findable: 'Your question about your State Pension forecast'. Never put personal data such as a National Insurance number or health details in the subject. For an email to a colleague asking for a decision, state the decision needed and by when. 'Decision needed by Thursday: new opening hours'. Open with the reason for writing or the answer. If you are replying to a complaint, acknowledge it and say what you will do. Close by saying what happens next, and who to contact. 'If anything is unclear, reply to this email or call me on the number below' is better than 'Do not hesitate to contact me'. If the email is going to a large group, ask whether it really needs to go to everyone, and use a mailing list or a Bcc where recipients should not see each other. If the message contains sensitive information, use the approved secure method and keep the detail out of the body of the email if you can. Always check the recipients one final time. Finally, remember tone. A short email can sound cold, so add a simple 'Thank you' or a brief greeting where it suits the relationship.

questions.prompt: You need a customer to send a bank statement by 6 June so you can process their claim. Which subject line is best?

options.text: Send your bank statement by 6 June to complete your claim
Your claim: action is required as soon as possible
Re: Claim 5521 - additional documents outstanding for review
Information we need from you regarding your recent application

questions.hint: A subject line should state the action and the date.

questions.prompt: You are replying to a customer about their State Pension forecast. Which subject line is best?

options.text: Re: query
Your question about your State Pension forecast
Your National Insurance number and forecast question
Reply

questions.hint: A clear topic helps the customer find the message and avoids personal data.

questions.prompt: Which subject line breaks data protection good practice?

options.text: Medical evidence needed for your claim, due by 6 June
Reference 4471: change to the time of your appointment
Medical evidence for Mr A. Khan, NI number QQ123456C
Your claim: documents we need from you by 6 June

questions.hint: Personal data should not appear in subject lines.

questions.prompt: You need your manager to choose between two opening-hour options. Which email opening works best?

options.text: Following our recent discussions, I have been giving thought to the various options for the opening hours.
I hope you are well. I wanted to touch base about the opening hours at some point.
I need your decision by Thursday on the new opening hours. Option A costs less; option B suits more customers.
As you know, there has been a lot of debate on the opening hours, so I wanted to share my views.

questions.hint: Stating the decision needed and the deadline helps the reader to act.

questions.prompt: Which closing line gives the customer the clearest help?

options.text: I trust this answers your query, and I remain at your disposal.
Please feel free to get in touch if there is anything else.
Do not hesitate to contact me should you require further assistance.
If anything is unclear, reply to this email or call me on the number below.

questions.hint: A closing that says exactly how to get help is the most useful.

questions.prompt: An email must go to 150 members of the public who do not know each other. What is the safest approach?

options.text: Put the addresses in the To field and ask them not to share
Put the addresses in the Cc field so that everyone is informed
Put the addresses in Bcc, or use an approved bulk mailing tool
Send the email in batches of 10 and use Reply all

questions.hint: Recipients' addresses are personal data and should not be shared.

questions.prompt: You must email a sensitive health letter. What is best?

options.text: Use the approved secure method and keep detail out of the email
Put the full letter in the body of an ordinary email message
Send it as a photograph taken from a personal phone camera
Send it to a personal email address for ease of access later

questions.hint: Sensitive data should go by approved secure routes.

questions.prompt: A short email you wrote to a stressed customer reads 'Send the form.' What would improve it most?

options.text: Add a long paragraph about the history of the form itself
Copy in a manager so the customer takes it more seriously
Add a greeting, name the form, give a date and say thank you
Write the whole email in capitals so that it stands out

questions.hint: A brief greeting and clear detail soften a curt message.

questions.prompt: Just before sending, you notice the auto-complete has added a person with a similar name. What is the best response?

options.text: Remove them and check every recipient's full address
Move them to Bcc and then send the email
Send it, because the system chose the name for you
Add a note saying 'sorry if received in error' at the end

questions.hint: Checking recipients prevents misdirected emails.

items.title: Answering the public: scenarios (Level 5)
items.source: Civil Service Code; ICO guidance; Equality Act 2010
items.body: Putting the principles into practice means making good judgement calls. When a member of the public contacts you, you balance helpfulness against the duty to protect personal data and to act fairly. Verify identity before you discuss a case. A husband phoning about his wife's claim, even with good intentions, is a third party unless she has given permission or holds a legal authority such as a power of attorney. Explain kindly, offer ways to give consent, and avoid confirming details. Where a caller seems vulnerable, for example in distress or at risk of harm, follow your department's safeguarding procedure and tell your manager at once. Do not make a decision outside your authority. Say that you will pass it to the right team, and explain what will happen next. If someone asks you to bend a rule for them, remember impartiality. The Civil Service Code requires you to act fairly and treat everyone equally, regardless of background. Do not give an opinion on ministers' policies. If the press or a journalist contacts you about a case, do not comment. Refer them to the press office. If a person asks for information that the department holds, that may be a Freedom of Information request, which must be answered within 20 working days, so pass it to the right team promptly. If someone makes a request in writing for their own data, that is a subject access request. Make a note of the date you received it, since the one-month clock starts on receipt. Record every contact accurately and objectively.

questions.prompt: A man phones about his wife's claim. He says she is ill and has asked him to call, but there is no record of her permission. What should you do?

options.text: Say the claim cannot be discussed without her permission
Confirm the details if he gives her date of birth and address
Tell him only the date of the next payment, with no other detail
Give him the claim status, as she is clearly unwell and cannot call

questions.hint: Without consent or legal authority, the claim cannot be discussed.

questions.prompt: A caller says they cannot go on and cannot cope without the payment. What should you do?

options.text: Transfer them to another team and give no explanation to them
Stay on the line, follow safeguarding procedure and tell your manager
Explain the complaints process clearly and then end the call
Tell them to ring back when they feel calmer and ready to talk

questions.hint: A person at risk needs a safeguarding response.

questions.prompt: A customer asks you to waive a deadline because they are a friend of a minister. Which principle matters most?

options.text: Efficiency: bending the rule saves a great deal of time
Impartiality: everyone is treated fairly, whoever they know
Speed: the case must be dealt with as soon as possible
Loyalty: friends of ministers should be given support

questions.hint: The Civil Service Code requires fairness and impartiality.

questions.prompt: A journalist phones asking about a named customer's case. What should you do?

options.text: Confirm that the case exists but give no further details
Ask your colleagues for their opinion before you reply
Do not comment and refer them to the press office
Give general details of the case without using the name

questions.hint: Press enquiries go through the press office.

questions.prompt: A person writes asking for 'all information you hold about me'. What is this request called?

options.text: A Freedom of Information request
A data breach report
A subject access request
A complaint

questions.hint: A request for your own data is a subject access request.

questions.prompt: When does the one-month time limit for a subject access request start?

options.text: When the request is received
When the person's identity is confirmed in person
When the data has been found
When the team manager approves it

questions.hint: The clock starts on receipt, so record the date.

questions.prompt: A caller asks what you personally think of a new government policy. How should you respond?

options.text: Say you agree with the policy, to keep the caller happy
Share your honest view, since the caller asked you directly
Say you disagree with the policy, so as to be honest with them
Say civil servants do not give personal views, and offer published information

questions.hint: Civil servants remain politically impartial.

questions.prompt: A customer says they find forms hard because of dyslexia. What is a suitable response?

options.text: Tell them the form is the same for everyone who applies
Ask what would help and offer adjustments, such as a different format
Ask for medical evidence of the dyslexia before you help them
Ask a relative to complete the form on the person's behalf

questions.hint: The Equality Act 2010 requires reasonable adjustments.

items.title: Checking a draft for errors before it goes out (Level 5)
items.source: GOV.UK Style Guide; GOV.UK content design guidance
items.body: Proofreading is more than spell check. A spell checker misses wrong words that are spelt correctly, such as 'form' for 'from', and cannot tell if a date, amount or name is wrong. Build a checking routine. First check the facts that matter most: names and titles, reference numbers, dates, amounts, deadlines and contact details. Check that the day of the week matches the date. In 2025, 14 March is a Friday, so 'Tuesday 14 March 2025' is an error. Check that numbers add up and match elsewhere in the document, such as an amount in the text and in the table. Check that the same thing is called the same name throughout. Check every attachment is the right one and is attached. Check the recipient and the address block. Check that the document does not contain personal data about anyone else, hidden comments, tracked changes or earlier drafts. Read slowly, ideally in a different format, such as printing it or increasing the font size, as familiar text hides errors. Read backwards, one sentence at a time, to check spelling. Let some time pass before the final check if you can. Ask a colleague to check anything important. Keep a record of your checks for high-risk documents, such as decision letters or letters containing payments. Finally, take responsibility. If you spot a mistake after sending, tell your manager and the recipient promptly and correct it.

questions.prompt: A draft says 'Your appointment is on Tuesday 14 March 2025.' What is the problem?

options.text: The year should not be written out in a letter like this
'Tuesday' should be written in capital letters in the text
The date should be written in figures only, as 14/03/2025
14 March 2025 is a Friday, so the day and date do not match

questions.hint: Check that the day of the week matches the date.

questions.prompt: A letter says 'We will pay you £450' in the text but the table shows £540. What should you do?

options.text: Find out which figure is correct and make them match
Use the lower figure in both places to be safe
Send it, because the table is more detailed than the text
Round both figures to £500 so that they match each other

questions.hint: Figures must be consistent and correct.

questions.prompt: Why does a spell check not catch the error 'Please send the form from Friday' when 'by' was meant?

options.text: Spell check only works on words typed in capital letters
Spell check cannot read the name of a day, such as 'Friday'
Spell check ignores any words that are under five letters long
Every word is spelt correctly, so the meaning is not checked

questions.hint: Spell checkers do not understand meaning.

questions.prompt: Which technique helps you notice errors in a document you have read many times?

options.text: Reading only the first line of each paragraph in turn
Reading it a good deal faster than before
Skimming it quickly on your phone while on the move
Changing the format, such as printing it or enlarging it

questions.hint: A different view makes errors easier to see.

questions.prompt: What should you check for before sending a Word document outside the department?

options.text: That the document is more than one page in length
Tracked changes, hidden comments and earlier drafts
That the file name contains some capital letters
That the font is Times New Roman in all the text

questions.hint: Hidden content can reveal sensitive information.

questions.prompt: You send a letter and then notice a wrong date. What is the best response?

options.text: Correct only the file copy and leave the sent one alone
Do nothing, as the date may not actually matter to them
Wait for the recipient to call you about the wrong date
Tell your manager and send the recipient a prompt correction

questions.hint: Prompt, open correction reduces harm.

questions.prompt: For which kind of document is it most important to keep a record of your checks?

options.text: A message wishing a colleague a happy birthday
A list of lunchtime options
A decision letter that involves a payment
A reminder about a team meeting

questions.hint: High-risk documents need an audit trail.

questions.prompt: A document refers to 'the Programme' on page 1, 'the Scheme' on page 2 and 'the Project' on page 3 for the same thing. What is the problem?

options.text: The three words are all written in capital letters
The sentences around them are all much too short
Readers may think they are three separate things
The document will not print because of the words

questions.hint: A single name should be used for each thing.

items.title: Spreadsheet scenario: monthly casework figures (Level 5)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: A team records casework each month in a table. Row 1 holds the headings: Month, Received, Closed and Within target. Rows 2 to 6 hold January to May. Received is 120, 100, 140, 90 and 110. Closed is 110, 105, 130, 95 and 100. Within target is 99, 84, 120, 76 and 90, which means the number of closed cases that met the service standard. The total received is 560 and the total closed is 540, so the backlog grew by 20 over the period. The average closed per month is 108. The percentage of closed cases within target is Within target divided by Closed. January is 99/110, which is 90%. February is 84/105 which is 80%. March is 120/130 which is 92.3%, the best month. April is 76/95 which is 80% and May is 90/100 which is 90%. Across the five months, 469 of 540 closed cases were within target, so the overall rate is 86.9%. This is not the same as the simple average of the five monthly percentages, because months are different sizes. To flag a month as growing the backlog you could use =IF(C2<B2,"Backlog up","Backlog down"). January has 110 closed against 120 received, so it returns Backlog up. February returns Backlog down. To count the months where at least 90 cases were within target, use =COUNTIF(D2:D6,">=90"), which returns 3. A formula for the percentage in row 2 is =D2/C2, formatted as a percentage. Always label the columns and units.

questions.prompt: Using the table, what is the total number of cases received from January to May?
What does the difference between total received (560) and total closed (540) tell the team?

options.text: The backlog shrank by 20 cases
20 cases were closed twice
20 cases were within target
The backlog grew by 20 cases

questions.hint: More came in than were closed.

questions.prompt: What is the average number of cases closed per month?
questions.hint: 540 divided by 5 is 108.

questions.prompt: Which month had the highest percentage of closed cases within target?

options.text: May
January
February
March

questions.hint: March was 120 of 130, about 92.3%.

questions.prompt: What formula gives the within-target percentage for January, with Closed in column C and Within target in column D?
questions.hint: Within target divided by closed gives the rate.

questions.prompt: What does =IF(C2<B2,"Backlog up","Backlog down") return for January (received 120, closed 110)?

options.text: Backlog down
TRUE
Backlog up

questions.hint: 110 is less than 120, so the test is true.

questions.prompt: What does =COUNTIF(D2:D6,">=90") return for Within target figures of 99, 84, 120, 76 and 90?
questions.hint: 99, 120 and 90 are each 90 or more.

questions.prompt: The overall within-target rate is 469 out of 540 closed cases. Why does it differ from the simple average of the five monthly percentages?

options.text: Percentages cannot ever be averaged in a spreadsheet
The monthly percentages contain a few calculation mistakes
Months differ in size, so each month counts differently
The overall rate leaves out one of the five months

questions.hint: A weighted figure reflects case numbers.

questions.prompt: What is the overall within-target rate, to one decimal place?
questions.hint: 469 divided by 540 is about 0.8685, or 86.9%.

items.title: Spreadsheet scenario: staff list, lookups and pay grades (Level 5)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: A small team keeps a staff list in A1:D6 with headings ID, Name, Grade and Office. The rows are 201 Priya AO Leeds; 202 Tom EO Cardiff; 203 Aisha AO Leeds; 204 Ben HEO Newcastle; and 205 Carla AO Cardiff. A separate pay table in G1:H4 has headings Grade and Pay, with the rows AO 24000, EO 28000 and HEO 33000. These are illustrative figures only. To count the AO staff use =COUNTIF(C2:C6,"AO"), which returns 3. To count AO staff in Leeds use COUNTIFS, which applies more than one condition: =COUNTIFS(C2:C6,"AO",D2:D6,"Leeds") returns 2. To find the pay for a grade, use =VLOOKUP("EO",G2:H4,2,FALSE), which returns 28000. To put each person's pay in column E, use =VLOOKUP(C2,$G$2:$H$4,2,FALSE) and fill it down. The absolute reference on the pay table keeps the table fixed as the formula is copied. With pay in column E, =SUM(E2:E6) returns 133000, which is 3 AO at 24000, one EO at 28000 and one HEO at 33000. =SUMIF(D2:D6,"Cardiff",E2:E6) returns 52000, the pay for Tom and Carla. To show only Cardiff staff use a filter on column D. To sort by Office and then by ID use a multi-level sort. Sorting only the Name column would break the link between names and the rest of the row. If a grade in column C were typed with a trailing space, such as "AO ", VLOOKUP would return #N/A, and TRIM would fix it.

questions.prompt: In the staff list, what does =COUNTIF(C2:C6,"AO") return?
questions.hint: Priya, Aisha and Carla are AO.

questions.prompt: What does =COUNTIFS(C2:C6,"AO",D2:D6,"Leeds") return?
questions.hint: Priya and Aisha are AO in Leeds.

questions.prompt: What does =VLOOKUP("EO",G2:H4,2,FALSE) return?

options.text: EO

questions.hint: The pay for grade EO is 28000.

questions.prompt: Why is the pay table written as $G$2:$H$4 in =VLOOKUP(C2,$G$2:$H$4,2,FALSE)?

options.text: So that the table is protected from any editing
So that the formula returns amounts in dollars
So that the lookup becomes case sensitive
So the table does not shift when filled down

questions.hint: Absolute references keep the table fixed.

questions.prompt: With pay in column E, what does =SUM(E2:E6) return?
What does =SUMIF(D2:D6,"Cardiff",E2:E6) return?
questions.hint: Tom (28000) and Carla (24000) are in Cardiff.

questions.prompt: A grade is typed as "AO " with a trailing space and VLOOKUP returns #N/A. What fixes it?

options.text: Change FALSE to TRUE in the last argument
Sort the pay table in descending order of pay
Change the pay table to use amounts in dollars
Remove the extra space, for example with TRIM

questions.hint: Extra spaces make text differ from the lookup value.

questions.prompt: Which action would damage the staff list?

options.text: Adding a new row inside the table of staff details
Filtering column D to show only the Cardiff staff
Sorting the whole table by Office and then by ID
Sorting only the Name column, leaving the others in place

questions.hint: Sorting one column separates names from the rest of each row.

items.title: Spreadsheet scenario: why does my formula give the wrong answer? (Level 5)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: Much of spreadsheet work is working out why a result looks wrong. Start with what the formula refers to. If the data is in B2:B6 and the formula is =SUM(B2:B5), the last row is missed. Fix it by correcting the range. If you add a new row at the bottom, outside the range, the total will not include it, so insert rows inside the range or use whole-column references. If a division gives #DIV/0!, the divisor is zero or blank. You can show a blank instead by testing it, for example =IF(C2=0,"",B2/C2). If a formula copied down gives odd results, check for a missing dollar sign. For example =B2*B1 with the rate in B1 becomes =B3*B2 on the next row, so the rate must be fixed with $B$1. Check for numbers stored as text, which SUM ignores. Check for blank cells and zeros: AVERAGE ignores blank cells but includes zeros, so values 10, 20 and blank give 15, while 10, 20 and 0 give 10. Check that displayed values are not rounded by the format. If three cells each hold 1.4 and show as 1 because the format has no decimal places, their SUM of 4.2 shows as 4, even though a reader adds up 1+1+1 and expects 3. Using ROUND in the formula changes the stored value, whereas the format does not. If a lookup fails, check for trailing spaces and for numbers stored as text. If a filter seems to leave out rows, check for blank rows in the middle of the data, which can split the list. Finally, use Show Formulas to see all formulas at once and check them one by one.

questions.prompt: Data is in B2:B6 but the total formula is =SUM(B2:B5). What is wrong?

options.text: The range stops one row short, leaving out B6
The formula should start with a plus sign instead
SUM cannot add as many as five numbers
The data must be sorted before it can be added up

questions.hint: The range does not cover all the data.

questions.prompt: Which formula shows a blank instead of #DIV/0! when C2 is zero?
questions.hint: Testing the divisor avoids the error.

questions.prompt: A rate is in B1. =B2*B1 is copied down and gives wrong results on later rows. What is the fix?

options.text: Use =B2+B1 so that the rate is added on
Use =B2*$B$1 so the rate cell does not move
Use =B2*B$2 so the row number is locked
Type the rate into each of the formulas

questions.hint: An absolute reference locks the rate cell.

questions.prompt: A1:A3 holds 10, 20 and a blank cell. What does AVERAGE(A1:A3) return?
questions.hint: The blank is ignored, so the average is 30/2.

questions.prompt: If the third cell in A1:A3 is a zero rather than blank (10, 20, 0), what does AVERAGE give?
questions.hint: The zero counts, so the average is 30/3.

questions.prompt: Three cells each hold 1.4 but show 1 because the format has no decimal places. What does their SUM display?
questions.hint: The stored total is 4.2, displayed as 4.

questions.prompt: Why does the result of the previous question look wrong to a reader?

options.text: Displayed values are rounded, but sums use the full numbers
The cells hold text, not numbers, so SUM is wrong
The sheet is protected so the total cannot be seen
The SUM function has added together the wrong cells

questions.hint: Formatting changes the display, not the stored value.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between using ROUND in a formula and formatting a cell to fewer decimal places?

options.text: ROUND works only on whole numbers and not on decimals
They are identical, and give the same answers always
Formatting changes the stored value; ROUND changes only the look
ROUND changes the stored value; formatting changes only the look

questions.hint: ROUND alters the value, formatting does not.

questions.prompt: A filter seems to leave out rows below a blank row in the middle of the list. What is the likely cause?

options.text: The header row is missing from the top of the list
The rows below have been hidden by an earlier sort
Filters cannot handle more than 100 rows at a time
The blank row splits the list into two ranges

questions.hint: Blank rows can break the automatic data range.

items.title: Spreadsheet scenario: percentages and targets in reports (Level 5)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: Reports often use percentages and targets, and small misunderstandings can lead to wrong conclusions. Suppose a service target says 95% of calls must be answered within 10 days. If 1,900 of 2,000 calls were answered in time, the rate is 1,900 divided by 2,000, which is exactly 95%, so the target is met. If 1,880 were answered in time, the rate is 94%, so the target is missed. When a rate moves from 82% to 88%, it has risen by 6 percentage points. In relative terms, it has risen by 6 divided by 82, about 7.3%. Always say which you mean. To find a percentage of an amount, such as 12% of 2,500, multiply: 300. To find a whole from a part, divide: if 45 is 15% of a total, the total is 45 divided by 0.15, which is 300. Percentage changes do not simply cancel. A 10% rise followed by a 10% fall leaves you at 99, not 100, if you start at 100, because the fall is taken from the higher figure. When showing shares that add to 100%, rounding can mean the displayed figures add to 99.9% or 100.1%. A note can explain this. Be careful with small numbers. A change from 2 cases to 4 cases is a rise of 100%, but not large in real terms, so give the actual numbers too. Do not compare percentages from different base numbers without saying so. Label every figure with its date and source, and keep a clear difference between targets (what we aim for) and actuals (what happened).

questions.prompt: A target says 95% of calls must be answered in 10 days. 1,880 of 2,000 calls were answered in time. What is the outcome?

options.text: The rate is 96%, so the target is exceeded
The rate is 95%, so the target is met
The rate cannot be worked out
The rate is 94%, so the target is missed

questions.hint: 1,880 divided by 2,000 is 0.94.

questions.prompt: A rate moves from 82% to 88%. How should the change be described precisely?

options.text: Up 6 per cent of the original
Up 88 percentage points in all
Up 82 percentage points in all
Up 6 percentage points

questions.hint: The difference between two percentages is in percentage points.

questions.prompt: Roughly what is the relative increase in the move from 82% to 88%?
questions.hint: 6 divided by 82 is about 0.073.

questions.prompt: What number is 12% of a caseload of 2,500?
questions.hint: 2,500 multiplied by 0.12 is 300.

questions.prompt: 45 is 15% of a total. What is the total?
questions.hint: 45 divided by 0.15 is 300.

questions.prompt: A figure of 100 rises by 10% and then falls by 10%. What is the final figure?
questions.hint: 110 minus 10% of 110 is 99.

questions.prompt: Three shares are shown as 33.3%, 33.3% and 33.3%. Why do they total 99.9%?

options.text: Rounding each share to one decimal place loses a little
Percentages cannot ever add up to exactly 100%
The underlying data was entered wrongly by someone
One of the shares has been left out by mistake

questions.hint: Rounded figures may not sum to exactly 100%.

questions.prompt: A report says cases 'rose by 100%', from 2 to 4. What would improve it?

options.text: Give the actual numbers as well as the percentage
Round the 4 up to 5 so the rise looks smaller
Remove the percentage and give no figures at all
Remove the dates so nobody can compare with them

questions.hint: Small numbers can make percentages misleading.

questions.prompt: A manager asks you to compare 40% from a group of 10 with 35% from a group of 2,000. What is a sensible caution?

options.text: The first group should be ignored because it is small
The larger group will always have the lower rate
The groups differ hugely in size, so the first is less reliable
Percentages from different groups can never be compared

questions.hint: Small bases make percentages unstable.

items.title: Spreadsheet scenario: preparing a file to share safely (Level 5)
items.source: ICO guidance on personal data; NCSC guidance; Microsoft Excel help
items.body: Before you send a spreadsheet outside your team, check what it really contains. Hidden rows, columns and sheets are still in the file and can be unhidden by the recipient. Delete data that should not be shared, or create a new file that holds only what is needed. Check every sheet, including those in the background. Formulas may refer to other sheets or files that hold personal data. Replacing formulas with values, using paste special, can remove links, though you should check the result. Look for comments and notes, which may contain remarks that should not be shared. Check the document properties for the author's name and other details. If a workbook includes a pivot table, the source data is stored in the file's pivot cache, even if the sheet with the data is deleted, so take care. Charts built from a data sheet can also contain the data. Safer options are to share a summary table that has been copied as values, or to export to a PDF where the summary is all that is needed. If you are sharing statistics about people, small numbers can identify individuals. A table showing '1' case in a small village on a certain day could point to one person. Departments often combine categories or suppress very small counts. Remove personal identifiers when they are not needed, or replace them with codes. Use clear file names that do not reveal personal details. If the file must contain personal data, share it by the approved secure method, protect it with a password or encryption and send the password separately. Only send the file to people who need it. Keep a record of what was shared and why.

questions.prompt: You hide the column with customers' names and send the workbook to a supplier. What is the risk?

options.text: The file will become too large to send by email
The supplier cannot open the file because of the column
The supplier can unhide the column and see the names
The names are automatically deleted when it is sent

questions.hint: Hidden data remains in the file.

questions.prompt: Which approach is safest when a supplier only needs a summary table?

options.text: Copy the summary as values into a new file and share that
Send the full workbook as a password-protected file
Send the full workbook and ask them to ignore other sheets
Hide the other sheets and send the file

questions.hint: A new file with only what is needed removes extra data.

questions.prompt: You delete the data sheet from a workbook but keep the pivot table. What might still be inside the file?

options.text: Nothing, as deleting a sheet removes all of the data
Only the formatting of the sheet
Only the sheet names
The source data in the pivot cache

questions.hint: Pivot tables store a copy of their source data.

questions.prompt: A table of statistics about people shows a count of '1' for a small area. What is the data protection concern?

options.text: The number is too small to be interesting
A small number can identify an individual
Small numbers cannot be put in a table
The number should be shown in red

questions.hint: Small counts can lead to re-identification.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible way to deal with very small counts in a published table?

options.text: Add the names of the people to explain them
Round all of the numbers up to the next 10
Show the small figures in a much smaller font
Combine categories or suppress the small figures

questions.hint: Combining or suppressing prevents identification.

questions.prompt: Why might you check a file's document properties before sending?

options.text: They can contain the author's name and other details
They show details of the weather when it was saved
They are needed in order to print the document
They list all of the recipients of the file

questions.hint: Metadata can reveal details you did not intend to share.

questions.prompt: A file must contain personal data and must be sent to an approved partner. Which is the best approach?

options.text: Send it to the partner's personal email address instead
Upload it to a free public file-sharing site for them
Send it by ordinary email with the password in the same message
Use the approved secure method, protect the file and send the password separately

questions.hint: Secure transfer and separate passwords reduce risk.

questions.prompt: Which file name is best for a spreadsheet of customer complaints sent to a supplier?

options.text: Customers-home-addresses-and-phone-numbers.xlsx
Final-complaints-list-with-names.xlsx
Complaints-Mr-A-Khan-NI-QQ123456C.xlsx
Complaints-summary-March-2025.xlsx

questions.hint: File names should not reveal personal details.

questions.prompt: After sharing a file with a partner, what record should you keep?

options.text: A copy of the recipient's personal email
What was shared, with whom and why
Only the date it was sent
Nothing, because the file is gone

questions.hint: A record supports accountability.

items.title: Security scenarios: classification and handling (Level 5)
items.source: Government Security Classifications Policy; HMG Security Policy Framework
items.body: In practice, security decisions come up in ordinary moments. You need to decide quickly and sensibly. Start by identifying the information and its classification. If a document is not marked, think about what harm would follow if it were lost or seen by the wrong person. Most documents are OFFICIAL, and some need extra care and are OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE. A supplier may need some information to do their job, but only what they need, and only by an approved route. Printing at home is usually not allowed for OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE material unless your department allows it and you can store and dispose of the paper securely. Do not take work to places where it may be overheard, overlooked or lost, and do not leave bags in cars. If you find a document marked SECRET left on a printer or in a public place, do not read it. Take it to the security team at once or secure it, and report where and when you found it. If a colleague asks to copy OFFICIAL data to a personal USB stick, remind them that only approved encrypted devices are allowed, and suggest a safe alternative. If a visitor asks you to hold a door or says they have lost their pass, politely send them to reception. If a stranger on the phone asks for details about a case or a person, check who they are using a trusted route and refer queries to the proper team. If someone from the press asks questions, refer them to the press office. You are not expected to be a security expert, but you are expected to notice, think and report. Do not guess if you are unsure. Ask the security team.

questions.prompt: You find a document marked SECRET on a printer in an open-plan office. What should you do?

options.text: Put it in the recycling bin to get it out of sight
Read it carefully to see who it belongs to
Do not read it; secure it and report where you found it
Leave it where it is for its owner to come and collect

questions.hint: Report and protect it without reading.

questions.prompt: A colleague wants to copy OFFICIAL data to their own USB stick so they can work at home. What should you say?

options.text: Only approved encrypted devices may be used, so suggest another way
That it is fine if the files are not marked in any way
That it is fine if they put a password on the stick
That it is fine if they delete the files again afterwards

questions.hint: Personal USB devices are not approved.

questions.prompt: A person you do not know stands at the secure door and says they have lost their pass. What should you do?

options.text: Politely direct them to reception rather than letting them in
Let them in at once, as they seem quite genuine
Let them in now and tell reception about it later
Ask them to follow you in quietly through the door

questions.hint: Do not let people bypass access controls.

questions.prompt: A supplier asks for the full customer list when they need only postcodes. What is the best response?

options.text: Send the full list to save time
Refuse to provide any information
Provide only what they need, by an approved route
Send the list in a password-protected file by personal email

questions.hint: Share the minimum needed.

questions.prompt: Can you print OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE material at home?

options.text: Whenever the document is no longer than about 10 pages
Whenever you happen to be working from home that day
Only if policy allows and you can store and dispose of it securely
Whenever you have a printer that works at home

questions.hint: Home printing needs approval and safe handling.

questions.prompt: A caller says they are from head office and asks for details of a named person's case. What is the safest action?

options.text: Give the details if they happen to know your name
Check who they are by a trusted route and refer the request
Give the details but ask them to keep the matter secret
Give the details if they say that the matter is urgent

questions.hint: Verify unknown callers before disclosing anything.

questions.prompt: Which of these should you do when you are unsure how to handle a document?

options.text: Treat it as public until you are told otherwise
Ask the security team or the document's owner
Lower its classification yourself to be on the safe side
Make a guess based on how long the document is

questions.hint: Ask rather than guess.

questions.prompt: A colleague leaves a laptop bag visible on the back seat of a car. What is the problem?

options.text: It could be stolen, losing the device and papers
The car insurance may rise if there is a claim
The bag may become creased and so look untidy
The laptop could get too cold or too hot in the car

questions.hint: Unattended work items should not be left in vehicles.

questions.prompt: Which statement about your responsibility for security is correct?

options.text: Only staff with a security clearance must report anything
You are expected to notice, think and report
Only the security team is responsible for security
You need not report anything that seems a minor incident

questions.hint: Everyone has a part to play.

items.title: UK GDPR scenarios: requests, sharing and records (Level 5)
items.source: ICO guidance on the UK GDPR; Data Protection Act 2018
items.body: UK GDPR questions at work are usually about requests and sharing. A subject access request from the person themselves should be passed to the right team on the day you receive it, and the one-month clock runs from receipt. You can ask for proof of identity if you have reasonable doubt. The person need not give a reason. If their file includes information about another person, such as a neighbour who reported them, that detail may have to be redacted. If the police ask for personal data, do not just send it. Refer the request to the data protection team, who will check that the request is proper and that an exemption applies. If an MP writes on behalf of a constituent, the department can usually reply, because the MP acts for the person, but follow your procedure and check the case. A request from a family member needs the person's consent or legal authority. Before you share data with another organisation, check the lawful basis and whether a written agreement is needed. If you spot an error in a person's record, the principle of accuracy requires it to be corrected, and you should tell anyone you have shared it with. If someone asks for their data to be deleted, do not just delete it. Pass the request to the data protection team, as legal duties to keep records may apply. Do not keep personal data in your own notebook, desk file or personal email, because copies you make are hard to find and protect. Data in a team's shared drive should follow the retention schedule. Where you must collect new personal data, ask whether you really need it and tell people why you are collecting it.

questions.prompt: A letter from a customer asks for a copy of all the information held about them. What should you do first?

options.text: Pass it to the data protection team that day and note the date
Send them the file exactly as it stands in the system
Reply asking the customer why they want to see the data
Wait until a manager has time to read it properly

questions.hint: The one-month clock runs from receipt.

questions.prompt: The customer's file includes a note naming a neighbour who reported them. How should this be handled in a subject access reply?

options.text: Send the note on to the customer without any changes
Check whether the neighbour's details must be redacted
Remove the whole note from the file without any checking
Send the neighbour's contact details to the customer too

questions.hint: Third-party data may need to be protected.

questions.prompt: A police officer phones and asks for a customer's address. What is the correct action?

options.text: Refer the request to the data protection team to check it
Refuse and end the call without referring it anywhere
Give the address if the officer gives you a badge number
Give the address, because the request is from the police

questions.hint: Police requests are handled by the data protection team.

questions.prompt: An MP writes on behalf of a constituent about their claim. How should you treat the request?

options.text: Send the whole of the customer's file to the MP's office
Ignore it until the constituent writes to the department too
Follow your procedure; the MP usually acts for the constituent
Refuse to reply, as MPs cannot be sent any personal data

questions.hint: MP correspondence is usually handled with the constituent's interests in mind.

questions.prompt: You discover an error in a customer's record that you shared with another team. What should you do?

options.text: Correct it and let the other team know
Leave it, as it is the other team's problem
Delete the record
Wait for the customer to notice

questions.hint: The accuracy principle requires correction.

questions.prompt: A customer asks you to delete everything you hold about them. What is the right response?

options.text: Pass it to the data protection team, as legal duties may apply
Delete only the paper copies and keep the electronic ones
Tell them that it is never possible to delete anything
Delete it all at once, since the customer has asked you

questions.hint: Erasure is not absolute, so the request needs assessment.

questions.prompt: Why is it a problem to keep a personal notebook of customers' details at your desk?

options.text: It will make your desk look untidy to visitors
Notebooks are too small to hold any useful data
The copies are hard to find, protect and delete
Notebooks are not allowed to be used in offices

questions.hint: Uncontrolled copies create risk.

questions.prompt: A request for personal data comes from a person who says they are the customer, but you have doubts. What can you do?

options.text: Ask them to explain why they want it
Refuse to ever deal with them
Ask for reasonable proof of identity
Send the data and ask them to prove it later

questions.hint: Identity checks are allowed when there is reasonable doubt.

items.title: Phishing and fraud scenarios (Level 5)
items.source: NCSC guidance on phishing; Action Fraud guidance
items.body: Real cases are rarely obvious. Attackers study their target and copy genuine style. Consider an email that appears to come from a senior manager, sent from a personal-looking address, asking you to buy gift vouchers urgently and keep it secret. Several warning signs appear together: a sender who does not normally write to you, urgency, secrecy and an unusual payment request. Stop, do not reply, and report it. Next consider a message that says your account will be locked in 24 hours unless you verify your details through a link. Real organisations do not usually threaten to lock accounts this way. Go to the website yourself, using a bookmark, or contact the organisation through a number you trust. A supplier email arrives saying their bank details have changed, with a new invoice attached. The invoice looks right, but check the change using contact details you already hold, and follow your payment approval process. A call from someone saying they are from your bank or the police and asking you to move money to a safe account is a scam. Genuine staff would never ask this. Hang up and call back on a number you know after waiting a few minutes, preferably from a different phone. If you realise you entered your password on a fake page, tell IT at once and change the password using a trusted device. If you opened an attachment, disconnect from the network only if your guidance says so and report straight away. Time matters. In the UK, fraud and cybercrime can be reported to Action Fraud, and suspicious emails can be forwarded to report@phishing.gov.uk. Take screenshots, keep the original email, and write down times. Share what you learn so colleagues are alert. Never feel embarrassed. Attackers are skilled and anyone can be fooled.

questions.prompt: An email appears to come from a director, asks you to buy gift vouchers urgently and says to keep it secret. What should you do?

options.text: Do not reply or buy anything, and report it to security
Reply to the email to ask the director for more details
Buy one voucher first to see whether the request is real
Buy the vouchers, as the director is a senior manager

questions.hint: Urgency, secrecy and unusual payment requests are classic signs of fraud.

questions.prompt: A message says your account will be locked in 24 hours unless you verify your details through a link. What is the safest response?

options.text: Reply to the message with the details that it asks for
Forward the message to a colleague so that they can check it
Go to the website yourself via a bookmark, or use a trusted number
Click the link quickly to avoid being locked out of the account

questions.hint: Do not follow links in threatening messages.

questions.prompt: A supplier emails to say their bank details have changed and attaches a new invoice. What is the right action?

options.text: Check the change using contact details you already hold
Update the details and pay, since the invoice looks genuine
Pay half of the invoice to the new account, then check
Reply to the email asking them to confirm the new details

questions.hint: Verify changes through a trusted route.

questions.prompt: A caller says they are from the police and asks you to move your savings to a safe account. What should you do?

options.text: Hang up, wait, and call back on a number you already know
Ask for their badge number and then carry on with the call
Give them only part of the information that they ask for
Do as they say, because the police are always trustworthy

questions.hint: Genuine police and banks never ask you to move money.

questions.prompt: You typed your password into a fake login page. What is the first thing to do?

options.text: Tell IT straight away and change the password safely
Change the password later in the week when you have time
Wait to see whether there are any strange emails arriving
Close the page and hope that nothing happens as a result

questions.hint: Quick reporting and a password change limit the damage.

questions.prompt: A text says a parcel is being held and asks you to pay £1.50 through a link. What is the best response?

options.text: Pay the fee, then check with the courier later
Do not click the link, and report or delete the message
Reply to the text to ask which parcel it is
Click the link, because the fee is so small

questions.hint: Small fees through links in unexpected texts are a common smishing trick.

questions.prompt: A colleague says they feel embarrassed to report that they clicked a link. What is the best advice?

options.text: Tell only a friend in the team and ask them to keep it quiet
Wait for a few days, in case nothing happens as a result
Report it now, because anyone can be fooled and speed limits harm
Keep quiet about it so as to avoid any blame being given

questions.hint: A blame-free culture helps people report quickly.

questions.prompt: Which pair of signs together most strongly suggests an email is fraudulent?

options.text: An attachment and a polite tone throughout the email
Pressure to act at once and a request to bypass process
A subject line and a date in the header of the email
A greeting at the start and a signature at the end

questions.hint: Urgency plus bypassing process is typical of fraud.

items.title: Breach scenarios: what to do and who to tell (Level 5)
items.source: ICO guidance on personal data breaches; HMG Security Policy Framework
items.body: When something goes wrong, speed and honesty matter. Take a few common cases. You email a list of 60 customers' names and addresses to the wrong person. Try to recall the email, tell your manager and the data protection team at once, and note what happened and when. The team decides whether the ICO must be told. The 72 hours runs from when the organisation becomes aware of the breach, so telling the team promptly keeps the organisation within its time limit. You send a message to 100 people, with all their addresses visible in the To field. That is a breach, because you have disclosed email addresses to people who should not see them. You lose an encrypted laptop. Report it straight away. Encryption reduces the risk that data can be read, and the team will take that into account, but the loss must still be reported and recorded. You find a patient's health letter was posted to the wrong address. Special category data raises the risk, and the team will consider whether to notify the person affected. A breach has to be reported to the ICO unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to people's rights and freedoms. If there is a high risk to individuals, they must be told without undue delay. Every breach must be recorded, even those that are not reported to the ICO. Do not try to fix the problem quietly. Do not delete evidence. Do not blame others. Do not contact affected people or the wrong recipient on your own unless the team has told you to. Afterwards, the department will look at what caused the breach and what can be done to stop it happening again, such as new checks, changes to systems or training.

questions.prompt: You email 60 customers' names and addresses to the wrong person. What should you do first?

options.text: Write to all the customers yourself to say that you are sorry
Try to recall the email and tell the data protection team at once
Ask the recipient to delete it and then say nothing more
Wait to see whether the recipient replies to the email

questions.hint: Contain the breach and report it quickly.

questions.prompt: From when does the 72-hour period for notifying the ICO run?

options.text: From the moment when the breach actually happened
From the moment when the person affected complains
From the moment when the ICO first asks about it
From when the organisation becomes aware of it

questions.hint: Awareness starts the clock.

questions.prompt: You send an email to 100 people with all their addresses visible in the To field. What is the position?

options.text: It is a breach only if the message also contained bank details
It is a breach, as addresses were shown to people who should not see them
It is a breach only if one of the recipients complains
It is not a breach, since they all received the same message

questions.hint: Disclosing personal data to others without a lawful reason is a breach.

questions.prompt: You lose an encrypted laptop. What should you do?

options.text: Report it straight away, even though encryption lowers risk
Report it only if it held special category data on it
Look for it for at least a week before you report it
Wait, because encryption means nobody can ever read it

questions.hint: The loss must still be reported and recorded.

questions.prompt: A health letter has been posted to the wrong address. Why does this raise the seriousness?

options.text: Health letters are always larger than other kinds of letter
Health data is never counted as personal data under the law
Health data is special category data, so the risk may be higher
Post is always much slower than the same message by email

questions.hint: Special category data carries greater risk.

questions.prompt: When must the individuals affected by a breach be told?

options.text: Only if the individuals themselves later complain
Without undue delay, if there is a high risk to them
Never, as it would only cause them needless worry
Only if the ICO asks the department to tell them

questions.hint: High-risk breaches require telling the people affected.

questions.prompt: A breach is judged unlikely to risk people's rights and freedoms. What happens next?

options.text: It is only noted down if a complaint is later made
It need not go to the ICO but must still be recorded
It is ignored, because no risk has been found
It must be reported to the police within 72 hours

questions.hint: All breaches are recorded internally.

questions.prompt: Which of these should you NOT do after a breach?

options.text: Tell your manager and the data protection team
Write down what happened and when
Try to fix it quietly and delete the evidence
Follow the team's advice on contacting people

questions.hint: Concealment and deleting evidence make things worse.

questions.prompt: What happens after a breach has been dealt with?

options.text: The ICO takes over the running of the department
The matter is forgotten once the breach has been closed
The department studies the causes and what to change
The person responsible is always dismissed from their job

questions.hint: Learning from breaches is part of good practice.
